title: Photon Demultiplexing Using Spatial Routing
authors: Hashir Kuniyil, Asad Ali, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Spatial sectioning of the far-field noncollinear field from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is a promising approach for multiparty quantum communication. Although demonstrations with six pairs of users have been reported, the fundamental limits remain unknown. These include the maximum number of channels, the required degree of channel optimization, and the dependence on input parameters. In this paper, we provide a practical framework that answers these questions by connecting input parameters and invoking a design theorem. For a representative configuration, we realize 12 user-pair channels with routing consistency exceeding $0.9999$ at a $12\%$ reduction in photon flux. We further show that sectioning improves the accidental-coincidence budget linearly with the number of channels $N$, allowing the aggregate key rate to scale with the user count. These results provide a design strategy for spatial-division multiplexing of entangled photons analogous to the channel-spacing standards used in wavelength-division networks.
summary: This work establishes a theoretical framework for achieving high-capacity quantum communication by spatially multiplexing entangled photon pairs from SPDC sources. By analyzing the azimuthal correlation, the authors derive a capacity law that dictates the maximum number of usable channels. This provides a crucial design blueprint for scaling quantum networks using spatial-division multiplexing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental limits for spatial-division multiplexing (SDM) of entangled photons generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) for multi-user quantum communication.
main_result: They developed a design strategy showing that 12 user-pair channels can be realized with high fidelity, and the aggregate key rate scales favorably with the number of users due to the relative scaling of signal versus accidental coincidences.
method: The authors derived a practical framework by decomposing the pair correlation into radial and azimuthal channels, leading to a capacity law governed by the azimuthal entanglement resource.
model_or_system: The system is based on the far-field noncollinear field from bulk-crystal SPDC, where the entangled photon pair correlation is analyzed using polar coordinates and transverse-momentum conservation.
key_observables: Routing Fidelity ($\eta$), Photon Flux Reduction, Azimuthal Schmidt Number ($K_{az}$), and the aggregate secret key rate ($R_{key}^{agg}$).
important_parameters: The capacity is governed by the dimensionless parameter $w_0q_0$, which is independent of the crystal length.
main_assumptions: The framework is specific to bulk-crystal SPDC and focuses on the position basis, distinct from OAM multiplexing.
figures_summary: Figure 4 illustrates the residual routing error versus guard width, demonstrating the error suppression mechanism, and shows the relationship between error and retained photon budget.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical basis (SPDC noncollinear field) to deriving the capacity law based on azimuthal correlation, and finally analyzing the practical implications for key rate scaling and error suppression.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative design theorem for scaling quantum communication channels using spatial degrees of freedom, analogous to established standards in classical optical networking.

FIG. 3: Wedge segmentation of the SPDC annulus into N = 4 antipodal channel pairs. The far-field ring is divided into M = 2N = 8 equal wedges of angular width ∆Φ = π/N; each antipodal pair (e.g. A/A′, B/B′) forms one self-contained two-user entanglement channel. Light-shaded strips of width g at every wedge boundary are the guard bands of Sec. IV A: photons landing in these dead zones are discarded at the coincidence level, suppressing routing errors exponentially [Eq. (16)] at a linear budget cost of ≈2g/∆Φ. The prescription uniform wedges + guards sized by Eq. (17) is the optimal segmentation of a degenerate SPDC ring (Sec. IV B).

Circles are pair-level Monte Carlo with statistical error bars (logarithmic ordinate). (b) Residual error versus the retained photon budget A (g). The star marks a 5% guard, at which the Monte Carlo residual is (1.70±0.14)×10−6 (108 pairs) while 88% of the coincidences are retained.
